analysis.one_liner: Replaces big-money Senate campaigning with public funds, free TV time, and strict spending limits.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Wellstone with no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let Senate candidates choose a public financing track: they would cap their own spending (about $25,000 of personal money, and a few million dollars total depending on state size), accept individual contributions of no more than $100, and in return receive public funds, 90 minutes of free prime-time television airtime, and discounted campaign mailing rates. It also would have banned political action committees from federal elections, restricted party soft money, required 'stand by your ad' disclaimers, and barred sitting Senators from franked mass mailings in election years. Senate candidates who refused the limits would have to tell voters so in their own ads.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates without personal fortunes or ties to large donors could run competitive Senate campaigns on small contributions plus public funds and free airtime; voters would get more candidate advertising with clearer disclosures and fewer unlimited PAC and soft-money streams feeding campaigns.

how_it_helps.text: Eligible Senate candidates receive public payments, free broadcast time, and reduced postage rates in exchange for accepting spending limits, reducing dependence on large donors [S2][S3].
Individual contribution limits to Senate candidates would drop from $1,000 to $100, and multicandidate PACs would be banned from federal elections entirely [S2][S3].
Candidates who refuse the spending limits must state in their advertising, 'This candidate has not agreed to voluntary campaign spending limits,' giving voters that information directly [S3].

Political party soft money — unlimited contributions raised outside federal limits — would be brought under federal reporting and restrictions, and federal officeholders would be barred from raising money for tax-exempt voter-drive groups [S2].
Sitting Senators could no longer use taxpayer-funded franked mass mailings during an election year, closing a self-promotion channel incumbents had used [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the new Senate Election Campaign Fund and reimburse independent-expenditure races; broadcast stations give up 90 minutes of paid prime-time airtime per candidate; PACs, large donors, and self-financing wealthy candidates lose their main channels of campaign money.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates an appropriations-backed Senate Election Campaign Fund and authorizes spending, so partial public financing of Senate campaigns would be a new cost to taxpayers [S2][S3].
Broadcasters would be compelled to provide free prime-time airtime to qualifying candidates, shifting a cost onto the industry and potentially into programming decisions [S3].

The bill itself provides for expedited Supreme Court review of constitutional challenges and a provision voiding everything if key limits are struck down, an acknowledgment that its spending limits and restrictions faced serious First Amendment risk [S3].

With a $100 contribution limit per individual, candidates would have to raise from very large numbers of small donors, which opponents argued could favor candidates with intense organized support networks over broad-based ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: modest public money, free airtime, and discounted mail against sharply reduced private money in Senate races, which the bill's own findings said had created the perception that contributions sway official conduct [S3]. The public cost is real but small relative to federal budgets; the larger questions were constitutional durability and whether strict limits would actually weaken candidates' ability to communicate against outside spending. On balance the bill aimed squarely at reducing the influence of large donors and PACs over the Senate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee on day one, and nothing else ever happened to it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Wellstone introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, the opening day of the 104th Congress [S1][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Governmental Affairs [S5].
No further action — no hearing, committee vote, or Senate floor vote — was ever recorded before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Political action committees, large donors, and the existing campaign-finance system were untouched; broadcast stations kept paid airtime; and incumbents faced no new limits on their own fundraising channels. No candidate or voter gained, since the voluntary system never existed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PACs and large donors; the system unchanged

for.name: Sen. Paul Wellstone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 104th Congress and delivered introductory remarks on the floor; the bill drew no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to (chair: Sen. William Roth, R-DE)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never reported it out, held no recorded markup, or scheduled any vote; the bill died in committee.

against.name: 0 Senate cosponsors
against.role: The full Senate rest of the body
against.what_they_did: Not one other senator signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill without the multi-sponsor support campaign finance overhauls typically need to move.

sides.party_line_note: Only one senator (a Democrat) sponsored the bill and there were no votes, so the partisan shape of opposition was never recorded; PAC money and large donations flow through both parties.

industries.industry: Political action committees and organized big donors
industries.note: The bill would have banned multicandidate PACs from federal elections entirely and cut the individual contribution limit from $1,000 to $100 [S2][S3]. PACs exist to channel organized money to campaigns, and the bill would have ended that channel; defeating it preserved their role in Senate campaigns.

Eligible candidates would have received 90 minutes of free prime-time airtime plus discounted postage, a direct cost to broadcasters' ad revenue and postal margins [S3]. Broadcasters' interest in keeping paid candidate advertising ran against voters' interest in cheaper, more accessible campaign communication.

The bill would have barred national party committees from soliciting unlimited 'soft money' contributions and restricted how parties spend on federal campaigns, while allowing a capped $5,000 grassroots-activity contribution [S2]. Both parties then relied heavily on soft money, so restricting it ran against the parties' fundraising interests even as it served donors' disclosure rights.

industries.industry: Wealthy self-financing candidates and their families
industries.note: Personal and immediate-family spending would have been capped at $25,000 per cycle, ending the ability of a wealthy candidate to buy competitiveness with personal wealth [S2][S3]. This was the direct removal of a wealth advantage in Senate races.
